title: Watts and the Too-Tidy Street
description: A scruffy little dog with a shining secret discovers something strange on a perfectly tidy suburban street.

passages.text: On Buttonwood Lane, every house had a neat little lawn. Every lawn had a round little bush. Every bush looked as though somebody had combed it. Even the garden gnomes stood up straight. It was a very tidy place to live.

At six o’clock, the sprinklers went shh-shh-shh. At seven o’clock, the curtains went swish. At eight o’clock, the neighbors said, “Lovely evening,” in almost exactly the same voice. But one resident of Buttonwood Lane was not especially tidy. His name was Watts.

Watts was a little golden dog with a scruffy chin and excellent running feet. He ran past the mailboxes. He ran around the bushes. Sometimes he ran in a circle because the circle was there. His ears bounced. His tail had opinions.

Watts also had a secret. Whenever he wanted, he could turn into a light bulb. A real, shining light bulb, bright enough to help someone find a dropped key or a slipper beneath a chair. Then he could turn right back into a dog.

But this evening he was enjoying being a dog. Dogs could sniff interesting corners. Dogs could investigate sandwiches. Light bulbs, Watts thought, probably did not get nearly enough sandwiches. He stopped beside a hedge and took a long, careful sniff. Something smelled wrong.

Not rubbish wrong. Not wet-sock wrong. This was a cold, dusty smell, like a cupboard nobody wanted to open. Watts lifted one paw. Across the lane, a porch light went out. Then another. Then another. Click. Click. Click. The street grew dark.

Beside the hedge stood a tall, thin man in a black hat and a long charcoal coat. He wore pointed shoes and long dark gloves. His shadow stretched across the pavement, although there was no light behind him. Watts gave a low, questioning woof.

The man raised one finger. From an empty house came three knocks. Knock. Knock. Knock. He raised another finger. The mailbox beside Watts began to whisper. “Nobody home,” it whispered. “Nobody home.” Watts knew that was untrue. He could hear someone snoring upstairs.

The man smiled a narrow smile. He curled his gloved fingers, and the shadows beneath the bushes curled theirs. Long shadow fingers crept toward the garden gates. Every time the man moved, something else on Buttonwood Lane became a little spookier.

A doorbell rang without anybody pressing it. A dark window seemed to blink. From inside an empty flowerpot came a tiny voice saying, “Behind you.” Watts looked behind him. There was his own bottom. He looked back at the flowerpot, thoroughly unimpressed.

“Woof,” said Watts. It was a small woof, but it meant something large: stop that. The man turned his cold gray face toward him. “Go home, little dog.” Watts planted all four paws. The man was frightening his neighbors. Watts would not go home.

Instead, Watts ran toward him. His feet pattered along the pavement. The man slipped around the round hedge. Watts ran around the other side. There he was again, standing perfectly still, with a shadow that would not stay still at all.

Watts barked twice. The man tapped his pointed shoe. The shadow under the hedge swelled until it looked as big as a bear. It had enormous paws and a crooked head. Watts stopped. His ears drooped. His tummy felt rather small.

Then Watts sniffed. No bear smell. No fur smell. No muddy, berry-eating, enormous-bear smell. Just the cold cupboard smell again. He leaned sideways. The shadow leaned sideways. Watts sneezed. The shadow did not sneeze. “Definitely not a bear,” Watts decided.

He took one step forward. The shadow slid away from his paw. Another step. Another sliding shadow. Watts could not catch it with his teeth. He could not pin it beneath his feet. But perhaps he did not have to catch a shadow.

Watts glanced at the dark porch lights. Then he looked at the long black shape beneath the hedge. He remembered all the things he had helped people find: the key, the slipper, a biscuit that had somehow rolled under a cupboard. He knew what darkness needed.

The man bent toward him. “Last chance, little dog.” Watts was frightened. He would have preferred a warm rug and absolutely none of this. Still, behind those tidy doors were people trying to sleep. He took one steady breath, ready to use his secret.

Pop! Watts became a light bulb. Golden light poured across the pavement and shone straight onto the bad guy. The man’s coat went thin. His pointed shoes faded. His hat dissolved into wisps. And then, exactly where the light touched him, the bad guy disappeared.

He was gone. Entirely gone. No hat behind the hedge. No shoes beside the gate. No long glove waving from a flowerpot. Watts shone on the place where he had stood. There was only a fallen leaf and a perfectly ordinary bit of pavement.

The whispering mailbox stopped whispering. The empty flowerpot stopped talking. The shadow beneath the bush became the proper size for a bush, which was a great relief to everybody, especially the bush. Nothing knocked inside the empty house. Buttonwood Lane was quiet again.

Watts stayed a bulb for a little longer. He lit the corner by the hedge. He lit the garden gate. He lit the pavement all the way to the nearest doorstep. Everything had its own ordinary shadow again, and every ordinary shadow behaved itself.

From inside a house, somebody whispered, “Is it over?” “I think so,” another voice replied. Watts gave his warmest glow. It was difficult to wag a tail when you did not have one, but he did his best to shine in a reassuring sort of way.

Pop! Watts was a dog again. Doors opened, and three neighbors came outside in their pajamas. A grandmother wore a lavender dressing gown. A father had striped sleeves. A little child in yellow pajamas peered around his leg. Watts sat down beside a low wall.

“Was that you?” the child asked. Watts wagged. “The shining?” Watts wagged harder. “And the spooky man?” Watts looked toward the empty corner, then back at the child. The child crouched and held out a hand. Watts pressed his scruffy chin into it.

“Good dog,” said the grandmother. “Very good dog,” said the father. Watts leaned against the child for a scratch behind the ears. That was one of the best parts of being a dog again. Light bulbs did not have ears to scratch.

Someone brought a biscuit. Watts accepted it politely, which meant he waited almost a whole second. As he crunched, his tail knocked a flowerpot slightly sideways. Everyone looked at the crooked pot. On Buttonwood Lane, flowerpots were never crooked. Watts held very still.

Then the grandmother laughed. The father laughed too. The child giggled and gave Watts another scratch. Nobody straightened the flowerpot. It looked rather cheerful that way. Warm lights shone from the porches, and the neighbors lingered together beneath the stars.

At last, everybody said goodnight. Their voices sounded different now: one sleepy, one cheerful, one enormous yawn. Watts curled up beside the garden wall while the child rested a hand on his back. The lane was peaceful. His paws were tired. His tummy was pleasantly biscuit-shaped.

Watts had been a dog, and then a light bulb, and then a dog again. Now he had another important job: to dream about running. His ears twitched. His feet gave a tiny patter in his sleep. And the slightly crooked flowerpot stayed exactly where it was.

scenes.alt: Watts trots down a perfectly tidy suburban street at dusk.
Watts watches a tall shadowy man beside the tidy houses at night.
Watts becomes a golden light bulb, and the bad guy disappears in its light.
Watts glows above an empty, peaceful sidewalk after the bad guy vanishes.
Watts is a dog again as his neighbors gather on the peaceful street.
